teacher_scientific_or_fidelity_note: Viscosity describes internal momentum transfer/friction between neighboring fluid layers; this item tests recognition rather than independently explaining why a real fluid is viscous.

review_theme: η textbook symbol attribution requires printed-source check
teacher_scientific_or_fidelity_note: Teacher-prepared source says the NBF section uses η for the coefficient of dynamic viscosity; that convention is scientifically valid, but printed NBF pp.91–95 have not been directly inspected and textbook-exact attribution remains pending.
1 Pa·s equals 1 N·s·m⁻² and 1 kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹; the distractor Pa/s has dimensions of pressure change rate, not viscosity.
Pa·s = (N/m²)·s = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹, using N=kg·m·s⁻².
Most ordinary liquids become less dynamically viscous on heating, though composition or phase changes can invalidate an unrestricted general claim.
For many common gases under typical conditions, dynamic viscosity generally rises with temperature, contrasting with ordinary liquid behavior.

review_theme: Flow rate is not determined by viscosity alone
teacher_scientific_or_fidelity_note: Honey generally has much greater viscosity than water at comparable temperature, but 'flows more slowly' assumes comparable geometry, pressure/head, volume and temperature; viscosity alone does not set a universal flow speed for unrelated arrangements.
Gases and liquids are both fluids; naming this pair is a foundational recall check rather than a direct assessment of explaining the origins of viscosity.
Drag is a resistive force due to relative motion through a fluid; a body at rest with respect to its surrounding still fluid has no motion drag in the simple model.
Drag is opposed to relative velocity of the body and fluid; it is not necessarily upward if the body moves upward or fluid flow is not stationary.
Aerodynamic drag names fluid resistance in air; does not imply that aerodynamic resistance is limited to one orientation.
Hydrodynamic drag is the general label used here for liquid-flow resistance, such as a moving object in water.

F_d=6πηrv is for a small rigid sphere moving slowly relative to an approximately Newtonian fluid in a creeping-flow/low-Reynolds-number regime; not a universal drag law for fast objects or non-spherical shapes.
The Stokes drag expression has no explicit g, although gravity can indirectly influence relative speed in a falling-body system; the question explicitly asks what is absent from the formula.
Drag is a force measured in newtons; η·r·v has dimensions kg·m·s⁻².
For fixed dynamic viscosity and sphere radius within the creeping-flow regime, F_d∝relative speed v.
For the same viscosity and relative speed in a valid Stokes regime, drag F_d is directly proportional to radius r; compare spheres while maintaining applicability.

review_theme: Terminal speed is nonzero constant velocity
teacher_scientific_or_fidelity_note: A falling body moving at terminal velocity still moves downward with constant speed while net force is zero; effective downward force includes weight minus buoyancy if buoyancy is retained.
The stem explicitly neglects fluid buoyancy, so F_d=mg at terminal speed; when buoyancy is significant, drag instead balances weight minus buoyant force.
Constant terminal velocity implies a=0, not v=0; drag balances downward effective weight in the model.
